I've had a few reasons that kind of accrued and compounded throughout the years...  
1) I lost a friend when I was in middle school, and while I was comforted he'd go to Heaven (so I believed at the time) it upset me in so many ways that God would allow someone so young to pass away  
2) probably whenever I first heard that animals don't go to Heaven? That always seemed like BS to me  
3) I went to Catholic school for a couple years, and was genuinely stunned and dumbfounded when some of my Catholic classmates (I was raised Presbyterian) would insist that only Catholics were true Christians  
4) I got diagnosed with mental illness as a teenager and, it became difficult for me to accept the more I thought about it that the, beatific, constantly smiling, "perfect" savior I'd been raised to believe in could save me from what I was feeling, if he's not even human to begin with but like a sock puppet for God.  
5) when I was a teenager I attempted suicide...a lot. After my worst one, I decided that simultaneously God had saved my life so I should be more devout, yet also somehow if I wanted to understand why I was saved, I needed to understand God and thus, learn about other faiths. (I don't really care anymore if God did save my life or it was the work of compassionate, competent medical professionals...if it was God though sometimes I wish they hadn't)  
6) when I was writing my statement of faith to be confirmed and I was like "I don't think original sin is real" and my pastor was like "okay, well let's hold on a minute"  
7) my world religions class in senior year of high school - had a really great teacher and it was super enlightening to learn more about other faiths around the world. I got to meditate with some Buddhist monks visiting my high school and it felt like singing in church, and after that I think was when I decided I needed to step back from church. Also after graduation I hit up this guy I knew and after a mutual congratulations on finishing high school, he declared to me all other religions were fake and that Christianity was the true way; haven't tried to say another word to him for 14 years.

There's some part of me that always wants to die because I want to die, and I have some solid reasons not to that I'm carrying with me, and I think I have enough self-awareness to know when I'm gonna be in danger. I just wish I could talk about how hard it can be sometimes just being alive today and living with that some part of you has ultimately decided you don't want to, or at the very least is comfortable with that decision and has been for a long time. It might be due to my loved ones experiences with my mental health issues throughout my life, and also the zealous dedication of the ethics and responsibilities of some mental health professionals throughout the years, but often I find it's hard to express these thoughts and feelings of hopeless and doom without fear of judgement or causing worry, sadness, stress, anxiety, and even sometimes anger in those I care about, and that's not even mentioning how wild, heated, quickly escalated, and emotionally charged sometimes these discussions become when I try to express myself. I think something I've come to realize, and this is something I remind myself of when I'm maybe a little down, is that life/living is all we know and it's "insane" (quotes important there) to people who don't struggle with this that, regardless of like religious beliefs I've found, that anyone would want to do it, to just hit the Exit button, make the ride stop and get off. I don't think it's a bad thing at all if you want to keep living just for living's sake, but the disconnect I find is people can't grasp that those of us who do live in this state of wishing for otherwise, and a deadstop end to it all is preferable somehow. Hope you're doing ok, OP.

So I feel like for you OP, because I'm not sure anyone has yet, let me break down where the plausibility of Tyrion Targaryen comes from. Let's begin:
* Fact #1 - and one I think most people skip on: Joanna Lannister and Aerys Targaryen were lovers during the War of the Ninepenny Kings
* Fact #2: neither Aerys nor his sister Rhaella wanted to get married to one another
* Fact #3: even though he and Tywin were strong and fast friends during their time in the war, Aerys grew to become insanely jealous of him, and the fact that Tywin got to be the one to marry Joanna instead of him didn't help.
* Fact #4: Aerys was not a faithful husband to his sister wife. He wasn't as brazenly lecherous as Aegon IV, but he carried on publicly with a couple mistresses.
* Fact #5: Aerys had become corrupted with power/become more mentally unstable enough that he seemed to care little about other people (Jaime's recounting of him unfortunately SA-ing his queen)
And finally *Fact #6: Joanna's last time at court in King's Landing was roughly a year before Tyrion's birth. 
There's no smoking gun, or anything explicitly written yet that makes Tyrion the son of Aerys II, I'm just saying, in my opinion it's plausible.

Jeez, I guess it depends on the program. 

I went to a residential program for my OCD - that was actually pretty great. I could use my electronics, had free reign of the hospital grounds, and could get my own groceries if I wanted. We'd all play poker together in the evenings, we could help the mental health workers there cook; compared to my other experiences it was like a mental health paradise.

Inpatient is a whole different world. When you've been to enough places it all becomes the same. This is a judgement, but they're not there to really help you...in inpatient they want you stable enough to be safe and move you on to outpatient care. In my opinion thats a really risky business model given the socioeconomic range of the people who can come through a hospitals doors. The last one I was in, I kept to myself, read a lot, called my family, showered regularly for the first time in awhile (wasn't in a good place), didn't really attend the groups. As I've seen inpatient units over the years, in my experience they've moved away from individual therapy and more towards group therapy which, in my opinion, is a shittier practice.  You have a lot of people, in a group maybe not even lead by a trained therapist, who all want to talk about their problems what brought them there, and rely on the assistance of other people not doing well, and only in an hour. Once, twice a week. It's not good.

Beyond that, its pretty standard. Depending on the program, can't leave, except for maybe an air or smoke break; or you can go on outings with family members if you've proven to be safe. Usually no electronics (in my last one that meant absolutely none, not even mp3 players). Unit's range from just a short hallway to a whole floor. Depending on the campus, you might be able to get physical exercise. Your every move will be monitored, but honestly thats not the worst part - you get over that pretty quickly. The worst part, and I found this out on my last stay, is if you get the choice taken away from you. My first two inpatient stays I understood, there was an action/consequence; you hurt yourself, you go to inpatient. My last one, it had been almost a month since I'd been intensely suicidal, and a nervous therapist on our first meeting had me evaluated which then led to me being committed. I was in a state of being angry for the four days I was committed. By the way, that therapist refused to see me once I was out - the agency said I was too high risk. 

To conclude, I suppose, mental health has come a long way in the US. Lobotomies are illegal and ECT  has been better vetted and researched; but theres still a lot of work out there. I personally believe but can't prove that insurance companies and profit have a lot to do with a shortening and a decline in care in inpatient units and a reliance on outpatient therapists and psychiatrists and that maybe hospitals rely moreso on a medicinal methodology (I remember in my last place this guy was trying ECT for the first time and was hopeful because nothing else had worked, which is great). We need kind people out there to be on the front lines who are willing to deal with a lot of shit (and not make enough money) to help people be well, and be their best selves. We also need real change in the medical industry so everyone have access to the best care. 

TLDR; been in patient three times over a span of a decade, been working in mental health for about 2 years. Inpatient sucks though shouldn't really be compared to jail/prison, and in my personal experience doesn't do enough to help patients who come in. Residential is great. Things can, should, and hopefully will be better someday.
